label: def:planar
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:planar}
A \emph{planar graph} consists of an oriented graph $(\mathcal V,\mathcal A)$ endowed with a fixed $2-$cell
embedding into the plane. Its \emph{faces} are defined by chordless cycles, 
and the set of its faces is denoted by $\mathcal F$.
head: environment
name: Planar graph

title: Remark
body_md:
The assumption of a $2-$cell embedding ensures that faces are well defined as 
$2-$dimensional objects whose boundaries correspond to polygonal simple closed curves in the plane. 
Although any embedding induces a rotation system on $X$ and thus a notion of faces, 
in general such faces need neither be finite nor closed, and therefore do not correspond to genuine $2$-cells. 
In particular, they would not support the homological framework required to develop 
the discrete differential calculus considered in this work. 
The cellularity hypothesis is thus both geometrically motivated by the class of 
locally finite periodic planar graphs studied below, and sufficient to develop a discrete Hodge theory.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Graphs satisfying the two conditions $\deg_0(X)<\infty$ and $\deg_2(X)<\infty$ will be referred
as graphs with bounded geometry. For them, the operators introduced so far are bounded.
We refer to \cite{Ke15} for the notion of unbounded geometry for graphs.
head: environment

label: prop_d1xi
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop_d1xi}
Let $X=(\mathcal V,\mathcal A,\mathcal F)$ be a periodic planar graph with bounded geometry. 
Then $\mathscr U_\mathcal F \mathrm d_1\mathscr U_\mathcal A^*$ is the multiplication operator from $L^2(\mathbb{T}^2,\mathbb{C}^\mathscr{e})$ to $L^2(\mathbb{T}^2,\mathbb{C}^\mathscr{f})$ 
by the real-analytic matrix-valued function $\mathrm d_1(\cdot):\mathbb{T}^2\to M_{\mathscr{f}\times \mathscr{e}}(\mathbb{C})$ defined for $\xi \in \mathbb{T}^2$ by
$$
\mathrm d_1(\xi)_{ij} = 
\sum_{k\mid \omega(\mathrm e_k)=\mathfrak e_j} e^{2\pi i\xi \cdot \lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor}
- \sum_{k\mid \omega(\mathrm e_k)=\overline{\mathfrak e_j}} e^{2\pi i\xi \cdot \lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor}.
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\hat{\mathfrak{f}}_i=(\mathrm e_1,\dots,\mathrm e_n)\in \mathcal F_0$. Then for $\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb{T}^2,\mathbb{C}^\mathscr{e})$ one has
\begin{align*}
&\big[\mathscr U_\mathcal F \mathrm d_1\mathscr U_\mathcal A^*\alpha\big]_i(\xi) \\ 
& = \sum_{\mu\in \mathbb{Z}^2}e^{-2\pi i\xi \cdot \mu}\big[\mathrm d_1\mathscr U_\mathcal A^*\alpha\big](\mu \hat{\mathfrak{f}}_i) \\
& = \sum_{\mu\in \mathbb{Z}^2}e^{-2\pi i\xi \cdot \mu} \sum_{\mathrm e\in \mu \hat{\mathfrak{f}}_i}\big[\mathscr U_\mathcal A^*\alpha\big](\mathrm e) \\
& = \sum_{\mu\in \mathbb{Z}^2}e^{-2\pi i\xi \cdot \mu} \sum_{k=1}^n\big[\mathscr U_\mathcal A^*\alpha\big](\mu \mathrm e_k) \\
& = \sum_{\mu\in \mathbb{Z}^2}e^{-2\pi i\xi \cdot \mu} \bigg( \sum_{k\mid \omega(\mathrm e_k)\in \{\mathfrak e_j\}_j}\big[\mathscr U_\mathcal A^*\alpha\big]\big((\mu+\lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor) \widehat{\omega(\mathrm e_k)}\big)
- \sum_{k\mid \omega(\overline{\mathrm e_k})\in \{\mathfrak e_j\}_j}\big[\mathscr U_\mathcal A^*\alpha\big]\big((\mu+\lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor) \widehat{\omega(\overline{\mathrm e_k})}\big) \bigg) \\
& = \sum_{k\mid \omega(\mathrm e_k)\in \{\mathfrak e_j\}_j}e^{2\pi i\xi \cdot \lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor} 
\sum_{\mu\in \mathbb{Z}^2}e^{-2\pi i\xi \cdot (\mu+\lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor)} \big[\mathscr U_\mathcal A^*\alpha\big]\big((\mu+\lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor) \widehat{\omega(\mathrm e_k)}\big) \\
& \quad - \sum_{k\mid \omega(\overline{\mathrm e_k})\in \{\mathfrak e_j\}_j}e^{2\pi i\xi \cdot \lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor} 
\sum_{\mu\in \mathbb{Z}^2}e^{-2\pi i\xi \cdot (\mu+\lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor)} \big[\mathscr U_\mathcal A^*\alpha\big]\big((\mu+\lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor) \widehat{\omega(\overline{\mathrm e_k})}\big) \\
& =\sum_{j=1}^\mathscr{e}  \sum_{k\mid \omega(\mathrm e_k)=\mathfrak e_j} e^{2\pi i\xi \cdot \lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor} 
\sum_{\mu\in \mathbb{Z}^2}e^{-2\pi i\xi \cdot (\mu+\lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor)} \big[\mathscr U_\mathcal A^*\alpha\big]\big((\mu+\lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor) \hat{\mathfrak{e}}_j\big) \\
& \quad - \sum_{j=1}^\mathscr{e}  \sum_{k\mid \omega(\mathrm e_k)=\overline{\mathfrak e_j}} e^{2\pi i\xi \cdot \lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor} 
\sum_{\mu\in \mathbb{Z}^2}e^{-2\pi i\xi \cdot (\mu+\lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor)} \big[\mathscr U_\mathcal A^*\alpha\big]\big((\mu+\lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor) \hat{\mathfrak{e}}_j\big) \\
& = \sum_{j=1}^\mathscr{e}  \sum_{k\mid \omega(\mathrm e_k)=\mathfrak e_j} e^{2\pi i\xi \cdot \lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor} [\alpha]_j(\xi)
- \sum_{j=1}^\mathscr{e}  \sum_{k\mid \omega(\mathrm e_k)=\overline{\mathfrak e_j}} e^{2\pi i\xi \cdot \lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor} [\alpha]_j(\xi).
\end{align*}
One infers from the last expression that
$$
\mathrm d_1(\xi)_{ij} = 
\sum_{k\mid \omega(\mathrm e_k)=\mathfrak e_j} e^{2\pi i\xi \cdot \lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor}
- \sum_{k\mid \omega(\mathrm e_k)=\overline{\mathfrak e_j}} e^{2\pi i\xi \cdot \lfloor \mathrm e_k\rfloor},
$$
as stated.

title: Remark
body_md:
One of the interesting results obtained in \cite{KeTaWi24} is the fact that if we consider 
a periodically weighted version of the Laplacian on $(3.12^2)$, it is possible to have either $0$, $1$, or $2$ flat bands. 
However, the $1$ and $2$ flat-bands are disconnected in the space of parameters indexing such perturbations. 
It would be interesting to understand what happens now since we have three sources of flat bands at our disposal,  
and in particular since some flat bands coincide in value but have support in orthogonal spaces.

label: lem:eigenvectorsDm
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:eigenvectorsDm}
Let $X=(\mathcal V,\mathcal A,\mathcal F)$ be a planar graph with bounded geometry, and let $m\geq0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] Let $\lambda > 0$ and $f\in\ell^2(\mathcal V)$ be such that
$
-\Delta_\mathcal V f=\mathrm d_0^*\mathrm d_0 f=\lambda f\ .
$
Then the two vectors
$$
\Psi_\pm:=\big(f,\ \alpha_\pm\, \mathrm d_0f,\ 0\big)\in \mathcal H_{DH}(X)\ ,
\qquad
\alpha_\pm:=\frac{-m\pm\sqrt{m^2+\lambda}}{\lambda}\ ,$$
satisfy $D_m\Psi_\pm=\pm\sqrt{\lambda+m^2}\,\Psi_\pm$.

\item[(ii)] Let $\nu > 0$ and $h\in\ell^2(\mathcal F)$ be such that
$
-\Delta_\mathcal F h=\mathrm d_1\mathrm d_1^*h=\nu h\ .
$
Then the two vectors
$$
\Phi_\pm:=\big(0,\ \beta_\pm\, \mathrm d_1^*h,\ h\big)\in \mathcal H_{DH}(X)\ ,
\qquad
\beta_\pm:=\frac{-m\pm\sqrt{m^2+\nu}}{\nu}\ ,
$$
satisfy $D_m\Phi_\pm=\pm\sqrt{\nu+m^2}\,\Phi_\pm$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i)
We look for an eigenvector of the form  $(f,\alpha\mathrm d_0f,0)$, for an unknown $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. One computes directly, using \eqref{eq:Dmdef},
$$
D_m\begin{pmatrix} f\\ \alpha\, \mathrm d_0f\\0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix} m & \mathrm d_0^{*} & 0\\
\mathrm d_0 & -m &\mathrm d_1^* \\
0 & \mathrm d_1 & m
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} f\\ \alpha\, \mathrm d_0f\\0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix} (m+\alpha\lambda)f\\ (1-m\alpha)\,\mathrm d_0f\\ \alpha\,\mathrm d_1\mathrm d_0f\end{pmatrix}\ .
$$
The last entry vanishes since $\mathrm d_1\mathrm d_0=0$. The first two blocks impose
$$
m+\alpha\lambda=\frac{1-m\alpha}{\alpha}\ ,
\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad
\lambda\alpha^2+2m\alpha-1=0\ .
$$
Solving this quadratic equation in $\alpha$ gives $\alpha_\pm=\dfrac{-m\pm\sqrt{m^2+\lambda}}{\lambda}$, and the corresponding eigenvalue is
$$
m+\alpha_\pm\lambda=m+\big(-m\pm\sqrt{m^2+\lambda}\big)=\pm\sqrt{\lambda+m^2}\ ,
$$
as announced.

(ii) The proof is similar, by looking for an eigenvector of the form $(0,\beta\mathrm d_1^*h,h)$.

label: def:dual
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:dual}
Let $(\mathcal V,\mathcal E,\mathcal C)$ be the unoriented data for the planar graph $X=(\mathcal V,\mathcal A,\mathcal F)$.
The \emph{dual graph} of $X$ is the planar graph
$X^*=(\mathcal V^*,\mathcal A^*,\mathcal F^*)$ defined by the following unoriented data
$(\mathcal V^*,\mathcal E^*,\mathcal C^*)$~:
\begin{itemize}
\item The vertex set of $X^*$ is the set of unoriented faces of $X$, {\em i.e.}~ $\mathcal V^*:=\mathcal C$.
\item For any $\mathrm e\in \mathcal E$ such that $\mathrm e\in\mathrm f_1$ and $\mathrm e\in\mathrm f_2$, with $\mathrm f_1,\mathrm f_2 \in \mathcal C$,
an unoriented edge $\mathrm e^*\in \mathcal E^*$ joining the vertices $\mathrm f_1^*$ and $\mathrm f_2^*$ is created. 
\item For each vertex $\mathrm x\in\mathcal V$, the cyclic order of edges belonging to $\mathcal E_\mathrm x$
defines a chordless cycle in $X^*$, and consequently a unique element of $\mathcal C^*$.
\end{itemize}
